newsitem.title: USA: House Democrat offers electric restructuring plan.
newsitem.headline: House Democrat offers electric restructuring plan.

text.p: U.S. Rep. Ed Markey Thursday introduced a bill to encourage states to open their electricity markets to competition.

Unlike two Republican bills that would require states to break up local utility monopolies by a specific date, the Massachusetts Democrat's bill included no deadline. Instead, Markey's bill offered states incentives to open their markets.
It would exempt utilities from the Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA) and the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (PURPA) if the states where they operated deregulated their markets.
"Essentially, we are telling the utilities that if you eat some competition 'spinach,' we'll give you a very sweet deregulatory dessert," Markey said at a news conference.

The bill by the influential member of the House Commerce Committee called for a renewable energy credit trading system under which 10 percent of the energy used to generate power would have to come from renewable fuels or a utility would have to have credits for 10 percent of its output.

Green groups hailed the renewable energy provision as the best one proposed so far. Other bills have called for utilities to use renewable fuels for up to 4 to 12 percent of their energy, but the 12 percent figure included hydropower.

The bill also called for the government to limit sales of power from coal-fired power plants above their current generation levels, unless those plants were subject to the same strict pollution regulations imposed on new generators.
Investor-owned utilities have long pressed Congress to repeal PURPA and PUHCA, saying that the two laws limit their ability to compete in the changing electricity market.

PUHCA restricts utility holding companies from investing in other businesses, including natural gas firms, in order to protect investors from subsidizing unprofitable ventures outside a utility's main area.

PURPA requires utilities to buy a certain amount of power from independent power producers which use renewable energy or cogeneration. Utilities say they should not be required to buy power from independent power producers in an open market.

Industry officials are skeptical that electricity deregulation will move far this year because the issues are complicated and involve a $200 billion industry that has been largely controlled by state regulation.

But Rep. Dan Schaefer, chairman of the House energy and power subcommittee who is pushing legislation to open the market by the end of 2000, said Thursday he wanted Congress to pass a bill by the end of 1998.

"It is my goal to have a bill signed into law by the end of the 105th Congress that gives all customers a choice in electricity suppliers by a date certain," he said at his panel's fifteenth hearing on the issue.
